title: Anterior Vitrectomy: Mastering the Anterior Segment's Deep Cleanup
summary: Anterior vitrectomy is a crucial surgical procedure in ophthalmology, involving the removal of vitreous gel from the anterior chamber or pupillary plane. Essential for managing vitreous prolapse during cataract surgery, trauma, or to clear vitreous opacities, it safeguards against complications like cystoid macular edema and retinal detachment, preserving ocular integrity and visual function.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Anterior vitrectomy refers to the surgical excision and removal of vitreous gel located anterior to the posterior capsule or through the pupil, typically involving the anterior third of the vitreous cavity. It is distinct from pars plana vitrectomy, which primarily targets the posterior vitreous. Its primary purpose is to clear vitreous from the anterior segment, prevent its incarceration in wounds, and manage complications that arise from vitreous presentation.

rows: Vitreous prolapse into AC, Dropped nuclear fragments/IOL haptics, Posterior Capsular Rupture (PCR)
Vitreous wick syndrome, Vitreous incarceration in wounds, Aphakic/pseudophakic pupillary block glaucoma, Cystoid Macular Edema (Irvine-Gass syndrome)
Vitreous hemorrhage in AC, Vitreous prolapse into corneal/scleral lacerations
Vitreous prolapse during penetrating keratoplasty, trabeculectomy, or tube shunt insertion
Management of dislocated IOLs (anterior chamber or sulcus fixed) with vitreous involvement

sections.title: 4. Fundamental Principles of Vitrectomy
content: **Infusion**: Maintains globe stability, AC depth, replaces removed vitreous. Typically via side port or limbal cannula (BSS, 60-80cm H2O).
**Cutting**: High-speed vitrector (600-5000+ cpm) minimizes traction by cutting vitreous before aspiration. Essential for safe removal.
**Aspiration**: Controlled vacuum (80-150 mmHg) removes cut vitreous and BSS, preventing excessive retinal traction.
**Port Size**: Commonly 20G, 23G, 25G. Smaller gauges often for limbal approach, larger for pars plana if needed.

sections.title: 6. Preoperative Assessment & Planning
content: **Comprehensive History**: Prior ocular surgeries, trauma, systemic conditions (e.g., Marfan's, pseudoexfoliation).
**Slit-Lamp Exam**: Assess anterior chamber depth, iris-lens diaphragm stability, signs of zonular weakness.
**Dilated Fundus Exam**: Rule out pre-existing retinal pathology (tears, detachments), especially in high-risk eyes.
**IOL Calculations**: If cataract surgery is primary procedure, determine appropriate IOL power and potential placement (bag vs. sulcus).
**Patient Counseling**: Discuss risks like CME, RD, endophthalmitis, and possibility of alternative IOL placement or secondary procedure.

sections.title: 7. Anesthesia Considerations
sections.content: Anesthesia choice depends on patient cooperation and complexity. **Topical/Intracameral** may suffice for straightforward vitreous prolapse during phacoemulsification. **Peribulbar/Retrobulbar** block is preferred for more complex or prolonged cases due to superior akinesia and analgesia. **General Anesthesia** is indicated for pediatric patients, highly anxious individuals, or extensive trauma cases requiring maximum globe control and patient immobility.

sections.title: 8. Surgical Technique: Limbal Approach (Post-PCR)
content: **1. Confirm Vitreous Prolapse**: Observe peaked pupil (after miotic), vitreous strands on instruments/wounds, difficulty with IOL rotation. Perform Seidel test on wounds if suspicious.
**2. Tamponade & Stabilize**: Inject high molecular weight dispersive viscoelastic (e.g., Viscoat) into the anterior chamber to push vitreous posteriorly and maintain AC depth.
**3. Create Ports & Infusion**: Establish 1-2 paracentesis ports (1mm). Place a 23G infusion cannula via a separate port or utilize an irrigating vitrector handpiece. BSS bottle height: 60-80 cm.
**4. Visualize Vitreous (Optional but Recommended)**: Inject ~0.1-0.2 mL dilute Triamcinolone Acetonide (TA, 4mg/0.1mL) into the anterior vitreous cavity to stain and highlight vitreous fibrils.

**5. Perform Vitrectomy**: Introduce vitrector (23G/25G) through a separate port. Set parameters: high cut rate (2500-5000+ cpm), low vacuum (80-150 mmHg). Always direct the vitrector port towards vitreous, away from retina, iris, and cornea.

**6. Thorough Vitreous Removal**: Sweep the anterior chamber, pupillary plane, and behind the iris/IOL (if implanted). Ensure all vitreous incarcerated in the main wound is freed using bimanual technique with a cyclodialysis spatula from the inside, while the vitrector is active.

**7. Verification**: Inject intracameral acetylcholine (Miochol-E) to constrict the pupil. A perfectly round pupil indicates a vitreous-free anterior segment. Gently dab all wounds with a non-fenestrated cellulose sponge; no vitreous should adhere. Elevate IOP transiently to check for vitreous prolapse.
**8. IOL Placement**: If primary cataract surgery, implant IOL in the sulcus or utilize an AC-IOL, often avoiding in-the-bag placement due to capsular compromise.
**9. Wound Closure**: Hydrate clear corneal wounds; suture if necessary to ensure watertight seal.

sections.title: 9. Surgical Techniques: Pars Plana Approach (AV Context)
sections.content: While anterior vitrectomy primarily uses a limbal approach, a pars plana approach may be necessary for complex anterior segment issues or posterior segment involvement (e.g., dropped nucleus, extensive vitreous hemorrhage, severe trauma). This involves creating scleral ports 3.5mm (phakic) or 3.0mm (aphakic/pseudophakic) posterior to the limbus. It offers superior access and control for deep vitreous removal and vitreous base dissection, but typically requires a vitreoretinal surgeon. Infusion, high cut rates, and controlled aspiration remain key principles.

sections.title: 10. Intraoperative Pearls & Pitfalls
content: **PEARLS**: High cut rate & low vacuum are paramount to minimize traction. Always use TA for visualization. Adequate infusion is critical for globe stability. Meticulous wound sweeping prevents incarceration. A perfectly round pupil after miotic confirms successful vitrectomy. Have a plan B (e.g., pars plana setup).

**PITFALLS**: Insufficient vitrectomy leads to CME/pupillary block. Excessive traction risks retinal tears/detachment. Incorrect vitrector port orientation can damage intraocular structures. Inadequate infusion causes hypotony. Proceeding with phaco after vitreous prolapse significantly worsens outcomes.

rows: During vitreous removal around IOL, insufficient support
Inflammation, vitreous traction on macula (Irvine-Gass syndrome)
Delayed traction, missed tear, insufficient vitrectomy
Vitreous incarceration in wound, chronic leak/inflammation

sections.title: 12. Postoperative Management
content: **Topical Steroids**: Potent corticosteroids (e.g., Pred Forte 1% qid-qid x 4 weeks, then taper) to mitigate inflammation and reduce CME risk.
**Topical NSAIDs**: (e.g., Bromday qd, Ilevro qd) significantly reduce post-operative inflammation and CME incidence. Continue for 3-6 months.
**Topical Antibiotics**: (e.g., Moxifloxacin qid x 1 week) for infection prophylaxis as per standard cataract surgery protocols.
**Cycloplegics**: (e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% bid-tid) indicated if significant inflammation, pain, or ciliary spasm is present.
**IOP Monitoring**: Close monitoring for early post-operative IOP spikes (e.g., from retained viscoelastic) or hypotony (e.g., wound leak).
**Fundus Examination**: Dilated fundus exam at 1-2 weeks, then periodically, to screen for delayed retinal tears or detachment, especially in high-risk patients.
**OCT Imaging**: If vision remains poor, consider OCT of the macula to diagnose and monitor CME.

sections.title: 13. RED FLAGS: Post-Op Emergency Signs
content: **Sudden, severe decrease in vision**
**Intense, unremitting eye pain (unresponsive to analgesics)**
**Marked photophobia or severe headache**
**Progressive redness with ocular discharge (suggestive of endophthalmitis)**
**New onset of floaters or flashes of light (potential retinal tear/detachment)**
**Persistent pupillary distortion or peaking**
**Signs of hypotony (e.g., very low IOP, choroidal folds on examination)**

sections.title: 15. Special Considerations: Pediatric Cases
sections.content: Anterior vitrectomy in pediatric patients (e.g., for congenital cataracts, Persistent Fetal Vasculature, aphakic glaucoma) presents unique challenges. Eyes are smaller, sclera is more elastic, and the vitreous is often more formed and adherent. Combined primary posterior capsulotomy and anterior vitrectomy are common during congenital cataract surgery to prevent posterior capsular opacification. A pars plana approach is often favored by pediatric ophthalmologists or vitreoretinal surgeons due to better control and reduced risk of peripheral retinal traction in these delicate eyes. Decisions regarding primary IOL implantation vs. aphakia are complex and age-dependent.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Future Directions
content: **Smaller Gauge Systems**: Evolution to 25G and 27G vitrectomy for anterior segment surgeons, allowing for smaller incisions, faster healing, and improved ergonomics.
**Ultra-High Cut Rates**: Vitrectors now operate at 10,000+ cpm, further minimizing vitreous traction and enhancing safety, particularly near the retina.
**Integrated Surgical Platforms**: Advanced fluidics, intelligent pressure control, and 3D heads-up display visualization systems are improving precision and safety.

**Pharmacologic Vitreolysis**: Ongoing research into agents that can chemically detach or liquefy vitreous, potentially offering non-surgical alternatives for conditions like vitreomacular traction or some vitreous opacities.

Sterile inflammation, severe corneal edema (limbus-to-limbus), fibrinous reaction. Onset 12-48 hrs. Minimal pain usually.
Inflammation, elevated IOP, visible fragments (may be difficult).
Chronic inflammation, hypotony, visible vitreous strand to wound, irregular pupil.
Surgical excision of vitreous to wound, wound repair
Pain, headache, nausea, corneal edema, firm globe. No significant inflammation or discharge.
Mild pain/irritation, expected AC reaction, responsive to standard steroids.

sections.title: 18. Prognosis & Key Clinical Pearls for Practice
content: **Prognosis**: Generally good, especially when performed for acute vitreous prolapse during cataract surgery. Visual outcome largely depends on the underlying cause and prompt, thorough intervention. Risk of CME is significant but often manageable.
**Prevention > Cure**: Meticulous surgical technique during cataract surgery minimizes PCR and subsequent vitreous prolapse.
**Don't Fear the Stain**: Always use dilute Triamcinolone Acetonide to visualize vitreous – it dramatically improves safety and completeness of removal.
**High Cut, Low Vac - The Mantra**: This fluidics setting minimizes vitreous traction, crucial for preventing iatrogenic retinal tears.
**Verify Vitreous-Free AC**: Utilize both intracameral acetylcholine (Miochol-E) to round the pupil and a cellulose sponge test on wounds to confirm no residual vitreous.
**Strategic IOL Placement**: If posterior capsular support is compromised, prioritize sulcus or anterior chamber IOL placement over in-the-bag to avoid complications.
**Aggressive Post-Op Anti-Inflammatories**: Prophylactic topical steroids and NSAIDs are critical to reduce the risk and severity of post-operative Cystoid Macular Edema (Irvine-Gass syndrome).
**Vitreous in the AC is NEVER Benign**: Always remove it completely to prevent long-term complications like CME, chronic inflammation, and glaucoma.
